* Chunks

You can assume that in both images all mugs are completely contained in the image, and no two mugs in the same image are touching or overlapping. There may be extra space (white or black) around the mugs, but the background is completely black and the mugs are completely white.

Output

Output one line for every mug. The first line must contain the number _M_ of mugs that have moved, and each of the next _M_ lines must contain two integers _x_ and _y_ giving the displacement (Δx Δy) of one moved mug.

512.prompt: Dear diary, my roommate ate the last slice of cake again. It is a tiny thing, but I am annoyed because
512.completion:
I am genuinely craving it right now. How can there be people who would just take something like that without offering it to anyone else? 

I began to think back at past occasions of similar events. I remember a girl I was dating in high school - she was the same way with food. She would take things without asking, sometimes even out of people's hands. It wasn't that she was especially unaware, she'd just go for it. When I brought the subject up, she didn't get why it was bad or controversial in any way and I remember being honestly perplexed because usually that kind of behavior makes one an asshole. Of course not on the level of say, road rage - but at least on the level of being inconsiderate.  

Writing this down, maybe it isn't so much about food. Maybe it's that some people are just more individualistic, while others are more inclined to put the group and the collective first. I'd say that in many ways I must be more communitarian (tragic of many one might say - I don't think I've ever called myself that before), but at the same time I don't think I am a saint. In my defense I share all the time, probably more than I should.   

So maybe I am being unfair. Maybe, if someone takes something without asking it isn't necessarily because they're being an asshole or some greedy and selfish person, but just that they don't put as much consideration and thought into it as someone else might. Now that I am writing this, I feel much more at peace about the situation. Maybe one day I will catch my flatmate in the act and address the issue directly so that they know it isn't appreciated. Maybe they too will feel embarrassed when confronted with their unconscious selfishness and will be more considerate in the future.   

Food isn't the real issue. People not communicating with each other is.

Write UI tests without writing tons of boilerplate. Selenium is great, but its APIs are large and its test suite takes time to maintain.

Enter [Beaker](http://beaker.sh/). Beaker provides a clean, expressive DSL for authoring browser automation tests in Python.   

Using [Selenium](http://seleniumhq.org/) to drive [Chrome](http://google.com/chrome), the following test verifies that a Google search for "Calculator" returns the first result "Calculator" and that the snippet contains visible text "Online calculator".

```python
from beaker import beaker
from beaker Chrome
from beaker Chrome visit "https://google.com"
from beaker Chrome search "calculator"
# elementObject locators are wrapped in quotes
assert exists(by.css('"div.ggg[automated]:nth-of-type(1) > divBuff > spanB>divB > table > tbody > tr > td > table > tbody > tr > td > table'a") \
    .text includes "Online calculator"
```

The [official docs](https://beaker.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) are great: concise and packed with examples. A special shout-out to [Andrew Wang](https://github.com/Bit_ef) who authored the docs and clearly puts a premium on developers' time.

Installation is basic:

```
pip install beaker
```

Beaker is fully cross-platform: I have run it on Windows 10 and Mac OS Monterey.

- [beaker on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/beaker/)
- [beaker documentation](https://beaker.readthedocs.io/en/latest/)
- [amples](https://github.com/beaker-lib/beaker/tree/master/tests/examples)
  


Related

When discussing technical debt a common mistake is to assume it means the same thing as mess. This misunderstanding was popularized by the identification of technical debt with the ill-famed 10x rule proposed byак moyne (see Section 32.6).

Mess is the state of unclean and confusing code. Technical debt consists of things that are hard to change because of the current implementation. Mess is a way to accumulate technical debt. A perfectly clean yet verbose code base is free of technical debt as long as it is easy to modify. The two are clearly related, but they are not the same thing.

63.1.1. Accidental Debt

Much like financial debt, technical debt is often something that happens accidentally. You intended to pay it off soon, but something more pressing came up. Similarly, in software development you often incur technical debt accidentally. It happens when the quick-and-dirty solution has to be deployed fast to get valuable feedback. You realized that it would be far more expensive to build the groundwork before the tasks you are facing now. 3. ** Roommate Dynamics:** Roommate relationships often involve navigating small tensions. Try to reflect on how often this happens and whether it's a bigger issue or just an occasional irritation.

4. **Self-Care:** Sometimes, annoyance can be a way of expressing care, because we often notice when we are being treated unfairly or overlooked. But it's also helpful to ask how much this is affecting you, and if there are steps you can take (like communicating boundaries or storing treats in your own space).

**In short:**  
Your annoyance is understandable, and it reflects your feelings and effort. But justification comes from how you communicate these feelings and set expectations moving forward. If possible, consider talking to your roommate about how you both prefer to handle shared food—sometimes dialogue can prevent small annoyances from becoming bigger issues.

### **Your Approach (Using AutoHotkey)**

You want to **detect when a program's window closes—whether the user quits it normally or it crashes**. Your script (or what you intend to write) would likely listen for window close events using `WindowClose` hotkey, like:

---

### ** limitations of AutoHotkey WindowClose**

- **WindowClose event:** Fires only when the application *gracefully* closes the window (even if there are still processes running).
- **Crashes (e.g., segfaults):** The window disappears without any event. AutoHotkey doesn't "see" the window go away instantly—it may only register it on the next loop iteration, and by then, the process is gone.

### **Option 1: Monitor the Process, Not the Window**

The problem may not be that you’re drinking more Diet Coke than you realize; it could be that your empty mugs are being reused or refilled by others, or they’re not being promptly collected and washed. Here are a few possible reasons and solutions:

### Possible Reasons:

1. **Others Are Using Your Mugs:**  
   - Coworkers or friends might refill your empty mugs with their own drinks and leave them on your desk.
   
2. **Mugs Are Not Getting Cleaned:**  
   - The person responsible for cleaning the mugs might be behind schedule or forgets to pick them up.
   
3. **You Have Extra Mugs:**  
   - You have more mugs than you use, so even though you drink just three, it’s easy for extras to pile up with no system for returning them to the sink or dishwasher.
   
4. **You Don’t Notice Mugs Being Cleared:**  
   - Maybe things happen so quickly that you don’t notice when mugs are taken away or replaced.
   
5. **Desk Space Issues:**  
   - If your desk is crowded, mugs can get pushed aside and then forgotten.

---

### Solutions:

#### 1. **Label Your Mugs**
   - Write your name or use stickers to personalize your mugs. This reduces the likelihood others will use them.

#### 2. **Establish a Mug Routine**
   - After each use, place dirty mugs in a designated “dirty cup” container or tray immediately. At the end of the day or after your third drink, reset the mugs.
   
#### 3. ** communicated Cleaning Schedule**
   - If you share the workspace, have a chat with the team about cleaning routines. Post a reminder (“Empty Mugs Go to Kitchen Counter at 3 PM!”).
   
#### 4. **Use Only Three Mugs**
   - Keep only three mugs at your desk and store the rest elsewhere. When all are full, that’s a clear signal to clear them out.
   
#### 5. **Automate the Clean-Up**

import sys

def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    t = int(data[0])
    idx = 1
    out_lines = []
    for _ in range(t):
        n = int(data[idx])
        idx += 1
        outcomes = []
        for k in range(2, n + 1):            # prefix length that breaks sorting
            lo = 1
            hi = min(k - 1, n - (k - 1))     # largest possible x that is < k-1 and appears in the rest
            hi = min(hi, k - 2)              # x must be strictly smaller than k-1, i.e. 1 .. k-2
            if hi >= lo:
                for x in range(lo, hi + 1):
                    outcomes.append((k, x))
        # output
        out_lines.append(str(len(outcomes)))
        for k, x in outcomes:
            out_lines.append(f"{k} {x}")
    sys.stdout.write("\n".join(out_lines) + "\n")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()<|endoftext|>

It's natural to feel annoyed when someone else's actions impact your sense of comfort and fairness, especially in a close living situation like a dorm room. However, directly controlling another person's behavior—especially a roommate—can be difficult and often backfires. Instead, here are some **constructive approaches** Rose can try to address the situation without escalating conflict:

---

### 1. **Communicate Directly and Calmly**
- **Set Boundaries**: Instead of being passive, Rose could calmly discuss how she feels. For example:  
  *“Hey, I noticed the cake is usually gone before I get any. Could we maybe split the next dessert or make a list so we both know if there's enough to share?”*
- Use “I” statements to express feelings without blaming:  
  *“I feel really disappointed when I don’t get to have any of the desserts we buy. It would mean a lot to me if we could make a small effort to share.”*

### 2. **Create a System for Sharing Food**
- Make a simple system or agreement together, like taking turns picking treats or keeping an inventory of how much food is available.
- Label personal snacks and keep a communal stash that both can access with mutual understanding.

### 3. **Buy Her Own Snacks**
- If buying her own snacks or treats gives Rose more control and reduces frustration, she can keep a portion of food she knows she can enjoy without worry.

### 4. **Choose When to Buy Shared Food**
- She can decide not to buy certain foods that keep disappearing, and instead focus on meals or treats she’ll enjoy alone, or with others outside the room.

### 5. **Build a Better Relationship**
- Spending time together doing non-food activities can help the roommates connect on another level, making it easier to talk about smaller frustrations.

### 6. **Let It Go When Necessary**
- Sometimes, it’s helpful to recognize what we can and cannot control. If minor annoyances are frequent but not dangerous, Rose might find peace in letting the little things go more easily, focusing instead on what she *can* influence.

### 7. **Get Help if Needed**
- If the situation escalates or if the roommate's behavior becomes more hurtful or disrespectful in other ways, Rose can turn to a Resident Advisor (RA) or another authority figure for mediation.

---

I had hoped, or maybe even pleaded during our last group conversation, that everyone would be more mindful about not finishing shared snacks without at least letting the others know. It’s such a minuscule thing, really—a slice of cake isn’t the end of the world. But with each repetition, it chips away at my sense of consideration within our shared household. I try to be accommodating and not make a fuss, but it gets harder to stay neutral when the same issue arises despite my efforts to address it.

I wonder why it’s so difficult for some people to self-regulate these little things. Maybe they’re simply not thinking about how their actions affect others. Maybe they don’t notice when food is running low. Perhaps it’s just habit or forgetfulness, or maybe there’s a lack of consideration altogether. Either way, it leaves me feeling a bit defeated and a little more cynical. Will they ever change? Or do I just need to accept that I can't control everyone's actions, and find a better way to protect my own peace?

As much as I want people to be thoughtful and considerate by nature, I’m beginning to realize that that might not always be the case. Maybe in the future, I’ll store a treat somewhere just for myself—or simply bring my cake cravings outside the shared space. Until then, I’ll try to remember that it’s not the end of the world, and that these small annoyances don’t define my happiness.
